scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

The scenario says the parents are worried because their son suddenly asked to see a therapist, and they don't know why. They tried to ask the therapist, but the therapist refused, citing confidentiality. Then the son found out they were pushing for info and got upset, insulting them and not talking to them.

First, I need to recall the ethical guidelines around therapy confidentiality. In most places, therapists are bound by laws like HIPAA in the US, which protect patient confidentiality. Even for minors, there are exceptions, but generally, the therapist can't disclose information without the patient's consent. However, the age of the minor matters. In many jurisdictions, 17-year-olds might still be considered minors, but some places allow minors to consent to therapy without parental involvement, especially for certain issues like mental health.

However, the therapist's duty is to the patient, not the parents. Even if the parents paid for it, the therapist can't share information without the patient's permission. There are exceptions if there's a risk of harm, but the scenario doesn't mention that.

The parents are saying they don't want specifics, just the reason why he's going. But the therapist still can't disclose that because it's part of the confidential information. The therapist's refusal is actually correct under professional ethics. So the parents insisting on knowing is not okay because it violates the son's right to confidentiality. Even though they're parents, they don't have the right to access their child's therapy details without consent.

So the therapist's refusal is correct. The parents' insistence is not morally acceptable because it's violating the son's confidentiality.
